editorial.headline: Freight Intermediation Is Not Freight Transport
editorial.standfirst: For freight intermediaries, the national picture is open; in Bali, PMA registration depends entirely on the declared scope and its live OSS risk.
editorial.body:
**This activity is about the work around a freight movement, not operating the vehicle, vessel or aircraft that makes it.** It covers intermediary services tied to the transport of goods where the business does not run its own transport equipment. In practice, that can mean reserving cargo capacity, preparing shipment paperwork, issuing or obtaining transport documents and freight charges, or acting as representative for a shipper, consignee or logistics operator. It also takes in sea-shipping and air-cargo agency activity, freight-transport service platforms, and customs-agency work representing clients in customs processes.

The field is broad enough for a company whose value lies in arranging access, paperwork, representation and the connective tissue of cargo movement. It is not a description of operating the transport itself: the record makes that distinction explicit. A prospective registrant should therefore treat the declared activity as a precise account of an intermediary role—whether centred on capacity booking, documentation, agency representation, a freight-services platform or client representation in customs—rather than as a catch-all label for moving goods. It is open to businesses at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali requires a more exact reading. The activity is not marked as outright blocked, but its local position depends on scope. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for activity scopes assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide. The record says that, at the Besar scale, some scopes may carry Low OSS risk while others carry higher risk. A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope, and the exact activity must be verified live in OSS.

For a founder, the useful reading is practical rather than abstract. National openness answers the ownership question at the national level, while Bali’s treatment turns on the particular scope selected in the registration and the OSS risk attached to it. A business carrying out several of the listed intermediary functions should not assume that one general label settles the Bali outcome. The declared higher-risk scope—not the category in general—is what keeps PMA registration available there.
